title: Reading Tertullian and Cyprian

objectives.can: Read Cyprian's balanced, clear periods and Tertullian's compressed, abrupt ones.

explanation.summary: Tertullian and Cyprian were both Christian writers of Carthage, and both wrote Latin that is unlike Cicero's. Cyprian builds clear, balanced sentences that carry you through a long thought; Tertullian writes short, sharp, crowded ones, full of images and exclamations. This lesson shows each style in real chapters and ends with a chapter of Cyprian.

sections.heading: Two African writers
body: Tertullian wrote in Carthage around the year 200. Cyprian was bishop of Carthage in the middle of the third century. Both wrote before the Vulgate existed, and both quote Scripture in Latin forms that are not Jerome's. Their works are among the earliest large bodies of Christian Latin prose.

In this library their English is matched only to whole chapters, not to single sentences, so the English edition is not shown beside the Latin. Rely on your own reading and on the notes here. The editions print no macrons and use *u* for consonantal *v*, so *uenire* is *venire*; one word is written *aput* where Cicero's spelling has *apud*.

sections.heading: Cyprian: the balanced period
body: Cyprian's sentences are long but clear. He sets phrases of the same shape side by side. In On the Lord's Prayer 1 the Gospel commands are 'nothing other than divine teachings', and then five nouns follow, each with a phrase of the same pattern: *fundamenta aedificandae spei*, *firmamenta conroborandae fidei*, *nutrimenta fouendi cordis*, *gubernacula dirigendi itineris*, *praesidia obtinendae salutis*. Each is a noun that names a support, with a genitive of what it supports. The list is built for the ear.

He ends a long thought on its verb. The first chapter's closing clause is *ut qui in tenebris mortis errantes inprouidi et caeci prius fuimus luce gratiae luminati iter uitae duce et rectore Domino teneremus*. Everything waits for the last word, *teneremus*, 'that we might keep'. In the middle, *duce et rectore Domino* is an ablative absolute with no participle: 'the Lord being leader and guide'.

He also uses plain connectives and antithesis to keep the reader oriented. In chapter 2: *ut aliter orare quam docuit non ignorantia sola sit sed et culpa*, 'so that to pray otherwise than he taught is not ignorance alone, but also fault'. A *non ... sed et* pair makes the contrast. Reported matters are in indirect statement: *iam praedixerat horam uenire*, 'he had already foretold that the hour was coming'.

In On the Unity of the Church 6 the pattern is shorter and sharper: *alienus est, profanus est, hostis est*, three clauses of the same shape with no connective, and then a balanced sentence, *habere non potest Deum patrem qui ecclesiam non habet matrem*: whoever does not have the church as mother cannot have God as father. The two halves answer each other: *Deum patrem* against *ecclesiam matrem*.

sections.heading: Tertullian: compressed and abrupt
body: Tertullian's On Baptism opens with an exclamation and no verb: *Felix sacramentum aquae nostrae*, 'happy the sacrament of our water'. The reason follows in a *quia* clause with an ablative absolute, *ablutis delictis pristinae caecitatis*, 'our faults of former blindness having been washed away', and a verb at the end, *liberamur*. Tertullian packs a lot into a few words and does not always give you the verb you expect.

He loves images and puns. Believers are *pisciculi*, little fish, who are born in water and are kept safe only by staying in it: *nos pisciculi ... in aqua nascimur nec aliter quam in aqua permanendo salui sumus*. The sentence turns on the repeated *aqua*. The text also names the Greek word for 'fish' (printed here in a corrupt form), which early Christians read as a code for the name of Christ.

In chapter 2 he addresses an abstraction: *pro misera incredulitas, quae denegas deo proprietates suas, simplicitatem et potestatem!* The speaker turns away from the reader and speaks to 'unbelief' itself; that is why the relative clause has a second-person verb, *denegas*, 'you who deny'. The next sentences are short and set against each other: *nos quoque ipsi miramur, sed quia credimus. ceterum incredulitas miratur, non credit.*

The result is a style that is easy to follow in the single clause and hard to follow across a chapter. Read it a clause at a time. Supply a verb where none is given, usually a form of *sum*, and look for the point of each contrast.

sections.heading: Scripture in an older Latin form
body: Both writers quote the Bible in Latin, but not in Jerome's Latin. At the end of On the Lord's Prayer 2, Cyprian has *reicitis mandatum Dei, ut traditionem uestram statuatis*. The Vulgate's version of the same saying in Mark 7:9 is *irritum facitis praeceptum Dei, ut traditionem vestram servetis*; in Matthew 15:3 it reads *transgredimini mandatum Dei propter traditionem vestram*. The meaning is the same; the wording differs, because Cyprian used an older Latin translation, or quoted from memory.

Another case: in On the Unity of the Church 6 Cyprian quotes the saying about being with Christ as *qui non est mecum aduersus me est, et qui non mecum colligit spargit*. The Vulgate in Matthew 12:30 has *contra me* where Cyprian has *aduersus me*, and *congregat* where he has *colligit*. And Tertullian in On Baptism 2 writes *stulta mundi elegit deus, ut confundat sapientiam eius*, where the Vulgate in 1 Corinthians 1:27 has *quae stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat sapientes*.

These differences are not mistakes. They are evidence of the Latin Bibles used before the Vulgate. When you meet a quotation, compare it with the Vulgate verse if you can, and notice where the words differ.

misunderstandings: Reading Cyprian's long sentences as loose. They are built: look for the parallel phrases and for the verb at the end.
Treating Tertullian's missing verbs as errors. He leaves them out for effect, and a form of 'to be' is usually understood.
Counting a difference from the Vulgate in a quotation as a misquotation. It is a different, older Latin form of the verse.
Expecting the English edition to help sentence by sentence. In these works the English is matched only by chapter and is not shown beside the Latin.

deeper.heading: Why Christian Latin sounds the way it does
body: Tertullian is among the earliest Christian authors in Latin whose writings survive in quantity, and many Christian turns of Latin are first found in him. Cyprian, writing a generation or two later, uses a more measured style, and later readers of Latin Christian prose have often taken Cyprian's clarity as a model. Neither writer wrote in a way that Cicero would have recognised; both knew Roman rhetoric and used it.

examples.analysis: A row of balanced phrases: *fundamenta* with *spei*, *firmamenta* with *fidei*, *nutrimenta* ... *praesidia* with *salutis*. Each is a noun naming a support, followed by a genitive of what it supports and, in most, a gerundive in agreement (*aedificandae*, *conroborandae*, *dirigendi*, *obtinendae*). The five phrases explain what 'divine teachings' are. Notice the same pattern repeated five times.

quoted.reference: Cyprian of Carthage, On the Lord's Prayer (De dominica oratione) 2
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: The end of the chapter quotes a saying in an Old Latin form: *reicitis mandatum Dei, ut traditionem uestram statuatis*. *reicitis* is a present, 2nd person plural, 'you reject'. *traditionem uestram* is the object of *statuatis*, a subjunctive after *ut*: 'that you may establish your tradition'. The Vulgate has other words for the same saying (Mark 7:9), a sign that Cyprian's Latin Bible was not Jerome's.

quoted.reference: Tertullian, On Baptism (De baptismo) 1
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *nos pisciculi ... in aqua nascimur*: *aqua* is the ablative singular, 'in water', and *nascimur* is a present deponent, 'we are born'. The clause that follows, *nec aliter quam in aqua permanendo salui sumus*, repeats *aqua* and ends on *sumus*, the verb of being safe. The sentence is a small image, one word repeated, and it ends in a rush.

quoted.title: On Baptism (De baptismo)
quoted.reference: Tertullian, On Baptism (De baptismo) 2
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *pro misera incredulitas* addresses 'unbelief' as if it were a person; *incredulitas* is nominative used for address. The verb of the relative clause is therefore second person: *denegas*, 'you who deny', with *proprietates*, *simplicitatem* and *potestatem* as the things denied. A few lines on, the sentences are short and set against each other: *sed quia credimus* and *non credit*.

quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *alienus est, profanus est, hostis est*: three short clauses with no connective. Then a balanced sentence in which each half mirrors the other: *habere non potest Deum patrem qui ecclesiam non habet matrem*. The subject is the relative clause *qui ... non habet matrem*; *potest* governs *habere*. Cyprian's clarity comes from patterns like this one.

options: Believers are sailors on a ship
Believers are farmers who need rain
Believers are birds that fly above water
Believers are little fish, born in water and safe only while they stay in it
check.explain: *pisciculi* is 'little fish'. The sentence plays on baptism as water: believers are born in it (*nascimur*) and are kept safe by remaining in it (*permanendo*).

quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: The Vulgate is identical in every word
The Vulgate has the opposite meaning
The Vulgate omits the saying altogether
The Vulgate has *quae stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat sapientes*: the same saying with different wording
check.explain: The wording differs (*quae stulta sunt*, *sapientes*), while the saying is the same. Tertullian's Latin Bible predates Jerome's.

options: It is a string of commands
A relative clause is the subject, and the two halves mirror each other: *Deum patrem* against *ecclesiam matrem*

options: It makes the three words conditional
It makes the three statements into one question
It shows that the verbs are in the future
It builds up three blunt charges in a row, each of the same shape
check.explain: Without connectives, the three short clauses of the same pattern strike one after the other. Cyprian is balanced and clear, but he can also be blunt.

quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: As a vocative address to the Lord
As an ablative absolute with no participle: 'the Lord being leader and guide'
check.explain: Nouns in the ablative (*duce*, *rectore*, *Domino*) with no verb form of their own make a free-standing ablative absolute. There is no participle of *sum*, so the sense 'being' is supplied.

options: An accusative and infinitive: 'he had already foretold that the hour was coming'
check.explain: *horam* is the subject accusative and *uenire* the infinitive: 'that the hour was coming'. This is indirect statement, with the subject in the accusative and the verb in the infinitive.

options: *non ... sola* against *sed et*: 'not ignorance alone but also fault'
check.explain: A balanced *non ... sed et* pair, with *ut* and a subjunctive for the result. This is Cyprian's habit of laying out a thought in matched parts.
